Bekhorot 38בכורות דף 38 · 26 October 2026ט״ו חשון תשפ״ז

Bekhorot 38 — Following the Sugya Across Both Amudimבכורות ל״ח — בעקבות הסוגיה בשני עמודי הדף

Bekhorot 38 begins by struggling to identify the exact measure implied by a hole and by defending that reading through a complex comparison between earthenware and other vessels. The Gemara repeatedly narrows its claims: from Torah law to rabbinic liquid impurity, from general comparison to a hekker-based analogy, and from broad language to locally fixed measures. On 38b the focus shifts to eye blemishes, where apparent contradictions are resolved by distinguishing black from white areas of the eye, tannaitic disputes are preserved, and procedural trust about who may identify a blemish is examined. The final sugya on permanent whitening and “waters” uses textual repair and seasonal clarification, but ends with a real unanswered question. Trust, Testimony, and the Authority to Decideנאמנות, עדות וסמכות ההכרעה

Across both amudim, the daf develops in stages. It first asks what kinds of testimony can be accepted in firstborn cases, including second-hand testimony. It then analyzes why a speaker may be believed when his own words both create and relax the restriction, and when “why would he lie?” works only against suspicion, not against established fact. Narrative episodes expose how trust can become publicly charged. The sugya next tests whether likely exposure makes kohanim or Yisraelim credible in reporting a blemished transfer, while preserving limits and exceptions. Bekhorot 35 — Following the Sugya Across Both Amudimבכורות ל״ה — בעקבות הסוגיה בשני העמודים

Bekhorot 35 develops in stages. It begins with classification of acts and consequences, then presents two mishnah-cases in which a blemish is initially permitted because it was not done with the relevant awareness, but later imitations are forbidden. The gemara then tests how far awareness extends through wording, indirect causation, and acts done in response to pursuit. Next it defines boundaries of birth and of visibility, showing that a defect need not be constantly visible to count. Across both amudim, the sugya repeatedly refines itself. It begins by including intentionally arranged indirect blemishing within the prohibition. Across both amudim, the daf develops by narrowing and re-narrowing each claim. It begins with Beit Hillel’s broad inclusion of additional eaters for a blemished firstborn, then tests whether distinctions from other areas of law can limit that inclusion. It turns from eating to handling, asking who authored restrictions on "margilin" and offering several non-identical explanations for them. Finally, it shifts to bloodletting a firstborn in danger, first comparing that dispute to doubtful terumah, then rejecting a simple analogy and grounding the core disagreement in scriptural readings about making a blemish.
